solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b swaps CRR reduction and OMO purchase descriptions, exploiting students who know both inject liquidity but confuse which is permanent vs. which has a collateral/securities dimension.
elimination_logic: Anchor on the clearest match: SDF (D) absorbs without collateral — description 4 (absorption without providing securities). Fix D-4.
CRR reduction (B) releases permanently held reserves — no securities involved, no reversal mechanism — description 2 (permanent injection without securities). Fix B-2.
OMO Purchase (A) involves RBI buying G-Secs permanently — description 1 (permanent injection via outright purchase of government securities). Fix A-1.
Repo (C) is temporary with repurchase obligation — description 3 (temporary injection reversed at maturity). Fix C-3. Correct matching: A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4 = option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: OMO and CRR are both permanent liquidity tools but differ in mechanism — OMO uses government securities; CRR is a reserve ratio change with no security transaction. Students who group them as 'both permanent' without the securities distinction will swap A and B. The conflation works because the outcome (permanent liquidity) is the same, but the mechanism is fundamentally different — which is what the matching question tests.
solution.final_explanation:
The four tools in this question represent the full spectrum of RBI's liquidity management architecture, classified by permanence and mechanism.

• A (OMO Purchase) → 1: RBI buys G-Secs permanently from the market — permanent liquidity injection through outright securities purchase. No reversal at maturity.
• B (CRR Reduction) → 2: Lowering CRR releases reserves previously locked with RBI permanently — banks can now lend those funds. No securities transaction; purely a reserve ratio change.
• C (Repo) → 3: Banks sell G-Secs to RBI with a buyback obligation at maturity — temporary liquidity injection that is automatically reversed. The defining temporary-reversible tool.
• D (SDF) → 4: RBI absorbs funds from banks without giving any collateral — uncollateralised absorption, the post-2022 effective floor.

Trap pairing: A and B are both permanent injection tools — the trap is confusing securities-based (OMO) with reserve-ratio-based (CRR).

Value Addition:
• OMO can also work in reverse (OMO sales) to permanently absorb liquidity.
• CRR currently does not earn interest for banks — hence cutting CRR is an earnings-positive event for banks.
• The combination of OMO + CRR manages structural liquidity; repo + SDF manages day-to-day (frictional) liquidity.

solution.concept_anchor: SDF replaced reverse repo as operative LAF floor post-April 2022
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (reverse repo as current floor) represents the pre-2022 understanding that remains deeply embedded in most standard textbooks; students who have not updated their knowledge to April 2022 will confidently select this.
elimination_logic: The question asks about the CURRENT effective floor — the key word is 'currently.' Post April 2022, SDF replaced reverse repo as the operative floor.
Eliminate option a — reverse repo was the floor before April 2022; it has been operationally displaced by SDF.
Eliminate option c — MSF is the CEILING, not the floor, of the LAF corridor.
Eliminate option d — the repo rate itself is the central policy rate, not the floor.
Option b (SDF) is the correct current effective floor of the LAF corridor.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a pure temporal-swap trap. Before April 2022, the reverse repo rate WAS the floor — and most pre-2022 study materials state this. Students who revised from older sources will select option a with high confidence. The SDF's introduction in April 2022 is a post-syllabus-freeze development that UPSC has incorporated into its question pattern. Knowing that SDF replaced reverse repo as the operative floor — and why (uncollateralised, more flexible) — is the precise update that distinguishes recent, rigorous preparation.
solution.final_explanation:
The LAF corridor's floor underwent a structural change in April 2022 with the Standing Deposit Facility.

• Option (a): Incorrect as of April 2022. The reverse repo rate was the operative floor until SDF was introduced. Post-SDF, reverse repo is formally retained but operationally sidelined.
• Option (b): Correct — SDF rate = Repo − 25 bps; since April 2022, it has functioned as the effective lower boundary of the LAF corridor.
• Option (c): Incorrect — MSF rate = Repo + 25 bps; it is the CEILING of the LAF corridor, not the floor.
• Option (d): Incorrect — the policy repo rate is the central reference point, not the floor.

Value Addition:
• SDF's key advantage: allows unlimited liquidity absorption without needing G-Secs collateral on hand.
• The shift to SDF reflected RBI's need to absorb the massive excess liquidity created by COVID-era stimulus without balance sheet constraints.
• Reverse repo rate (3.35% as of its last operative setting) technically still exists but is not the primary absorption tool.

solution.concept_anchor: COVID repo at 4%; reverse repo asymmetric cut to 3.35%; 2022-23 hike to 6.5%

statement_analysis.statement: The policy repo rate reached its historic low of 4 per cent in May 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic — a rate lower than any point reached during the post-Global Financial Crisis easing cycle.
statement_analysis.reason: Repo was cut to 4% in May 2020 (off-cycle meeting), which was indeed lower than the post-GFC low of approximately 4.75% reached in 2009 — making it a historic low at that time.

statement_analysis.statement: During the COVID-19 response, the reverse repo rate was reduced to 3.35 per cent — a cut of 90 basis points from its pre-COVID level — deliberately exceeding the reduction applied to the policy repo rate.
statement_analysis.reason: Repo was cut by 40 bps (from 4.40% to 4%); reverse repo was cut by 90 bps (from 4.25% to 3.35%). The asymmetric cut was deliberate — to disincentivise banks from parking funds with RBI.

statement_analysis.statement: The post-COVID rate hike cycle brought the policy repo rate to 6 per cent by the end of the 2022–23 financial year, restoring it to the pre-COVID level prevailing in early 2020.
statement_analysis.reason: The rate hike cycle raised repo to 6.5% (not 6%) by February 2023. The pre-COVID repo rate was approximately 5.15% — so 6.5% exceeded the pre-COVID level, not merely restored it.

statement_analysis.statement: The widening of the LAF corridor during COVID — from the standard 50 basis points to approximately 65 basis points — was a result of the asymmetric reduction of reverse repo rate relative to the repo rate.
statement_analysis.reason: Standard corridor: 25 bps below and above repo = 50 bps total. After cuts: repo at 4% and reverse repo at 3.35% = 65 bps gap (reverse repo 65 bps below repo). This widening was the direct arithmetic consequence of the asymmetric cut.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All four' is the dominant distractor; statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The error in statement 3 requires knowing the precise rate (6.5%, not 6%) and the pre-COVID level (~5.15%), which is a numerical precision test.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 3: 'repo raised to 6 per cent by end of 2022-23' — incorrect on two counts. The rate reached 6.5% (not 6%), and the pre-COVID rate was ~5.15% (not 6%), so it exceeded the pre-COVID level rather than restoring it. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1, 2, and 4 are all factually accurate — 4% COVID low, 3.35% reverse repo, 65 bps widened corridor.
Three correct, one incorrect — answer is 'Only three' = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 has a double error: the rate number (6% vs. 6.5%) and the characterisation ('restoring pre-COVID level' when repo actually surpassed it). Students who remember 'rates were hiked after COVID' may accept 6% as close enough without checking precision. The 'restoring pre-COVID level' framing adds a second layer of plausibility — since it sounds like a return to normalcy. Both errors require precise historical data recall.
solution.final_explanation:
COVID-era monetary policy produced two innovations: a historic rate low and an asymmetric corridor — both UPSC-relevant.

• Statement 1 — Correct: 4% repo in May 2020 was India's lowest policy rate on record at that time, below the post-GFC trough of ~4.75%.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Reverse repo cut by 90 bps to 3.35%; repo cut by 40 bps to 4%. Deliberate asymmetry to nudge banks into lending.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The hike cycle reached 6.5% by February 2023 — not 6%. The pre-COVID repo was ~5.15% — so 6.5% EXCEEDED the pre-COVID level by over 100 bps, rather than merely restoring it.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Gap between repo (4%) and reverse repo (3.35%) = 65 bps — versus the standard 25 bps spread, the corridor widened to 65 bps total (not the usual 50 bps symmetric corridor).

Value Addition:
• The 2022 off-cycle emergency hike (40 bps in May 2022) mirrored the 2020 off-cycle emergency cut in structure.
• Reverse repo at 3.35% was the lowest level ever for that rate.
• Each subsequent 2022–23 MPC meeting hiked by 50 bps until 35 bps and 25 bps increments signalled approaching terminal rate.

solution.concept_anchor: Real repo rate rising while nominal falls — contractionary effect in high-inflation context
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a ('monetary stance is expansionary because repo rate fell') is the partial-truth trap: the nominal rate did fall, which is usually expansionary — but if inflation fell faster, the real rate rose, making the stance contractionary in real terms.
elimination_logic: Calculate the real repo rate before: Nominal (6%) − Inflation (2%) = real rate of +4%.
Calculate the real repo rate after: Nominal (5.5%) − Inflation (0.5%) = real rate of +5%.
Despite the nominal rate falling by 50 bps, the real rate ROSE by 100 bps (from +4% to +5%) because inflation fell even faster than the nominal rate cut.
A rising real repo rate means the monetary stance became MORE contractionary (tighter in real terms), even though the nominal rate was cut. Option (d) correctly identifies this.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is the precise UPSC trap identified in the real repo rate key_dimensions: 'A LOWER nominal repo rate during HIGH inflation can still be contractionary in real terms if real rate rises.' The scenario reverses this: a lower nominal rate + even lower inflation = rising real rate = more contractionary. Students who anchor on the nominal rate cut and categorise it as 'expansionary' without computing the real rate will select option (a). The question tests whether candidates have truly internalised the real vs. nominal distinction.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the most counterintuitive aspect of real vs. nominal interest rate analysis.

Key calculation:
• Before: Real repo rate = 6% − 2% = +4%
• After: Real repo rate = 5.5% − 0.5% = +5%

The nominal repo rate fell by 50 bps — superficially expansionary. But inflation fell by 150 bps simultaneously (2% → 0.5%), causing the real repo rate to RISE by 100 bps (4% → 5%). A higher real repo rate means borrowing is more expensive in inflation-adjusted terms — monetary policy became MORE restrictive despite the nominal cut.

• Option (a): Incorrect — anchors on nominal rate only; ignores the larger fall in inflation that raised the real rate.
• Option (b): Incorrect — accommodative stance requires a declining real rate; the real rate rose.
• Option (c): Incorrect — the stance was not unchanged; it became materially tighter in real terms.
• Option (d): Correct — the real repo rate rose from 4% to 5%, indicating a contractionary shift despite the nominal rate reduction.

Value Addition:
• This scenario illustrates why RBI monitors real interest rates alongside nominal rates under FIT.
• During COVID, nominal repo was at 4% and CPI was often above 6% — real rate was negative (stimulative).
• The Taylor Rule (prescribes optimal real policy rates based on output and inflation gaps) uses real — not nominal — rates as its core variable.

solution.concept_anchor: Repo vs. reverse repo direction — who borrows from whom

statement_analysis.statement: Under a repo transaction conducted within the Liquidity Adjustment Facility, the Reserve Bank of India sells government securities to commercial banks and agrees to buy them back at a lower price, thereby injecting liquidity into the banking system.
statement_analysis.reason: The direction is reversed. Under repo, it is the commercial BANKS that sell securities to RBI (not RBI selling to banks) and agree to buy them back. RBI is the buyer/lender; banks are the sellers/borrowers. The buyback price is HIGHER (not lower) than the sale price — the difference represents the repo rate interest.

statement_analysis.statement: The Liquidity Adjustment Facility serves as both a liquidity injection mechanism (through repo) and a liquidity absorption mechanism (through reverse repo/SDF), giving the RBI a bidirectional toolkit for daily cash management.
statement_analysis.reason: This precisely describes LAF's dual function — repo injects and reverse repo/SDF absorbs, making it a complete bidirectional liquidity management framework for RBI.

statement_analysis.statement: A bank experiencing a temporary surplus of funds beyond its daily operational requirements would approach the RBI's repo window to earn interest on that surplus.
statement_analysis.reason: A bank with SURPLUS funds would use the reverse repo window (or SDF) — not the repo window. The repo window is for banks that NEED funds; the reverse repo/SDF window is for banks that HAVE excess funds and want to park them with RBI to earn interest.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (statements 1 and 2) as the NOT-correct pair would mislead students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong but mistakenly also flag Statement 2 as incorrect because they confuse 'LAF as rate' with 'LAF as framework.'
elimination_logic: The question asks which are NOT correct — identify the false statements.

Statement 1: Describes RBI selling to banks at a lower buyback price — both the direction (banks sell to RBI, not vice versa) and the price direction (buyback is higher, not lower) are wrong. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2: Correctly describes LAF as bidirectional. Statement 2 IS correct, so it should not be in the answer.
Statement 3: A surplus bank would use reverse repo/SDF, NOT repo. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — answer is option (b): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 contains a double error — the direction of the securities transfer AND the price direction (lower vs. higher). Students who know 'repo involves government securities and RBI' may not catch that the seller/buyer roles are reversed, or may correctly identify the direction but miss the 'lower price' error. Statement 3 exploits the word 'surplus' — students should know that surplus banks go to reverse repo/SDF, not repo. Conflating the two windows is the core trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the precise direction of repo and reverse repo transactions prevents the most common errors in monetary policy questions.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect (double error): (i) It is commercial banks that sell securities to RBI — not RBI selling to banks. (ii) The buyback price is HIGHER, not lower — the difference between buyback price and sale price IS the interest (repo rate). A lower buyback price would mean banks profit from the transaction, which is the opposite of the interest-payment reality.
• Statement 2 — Correct: LAF is precisely a bidirectional toolkit — repo for injection (when banks need funds) and reverse repo/SDF for absorption (when banks have surplus funds).
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: A bank with surplus funds accesses the reverse repo window (or SDF post-2022) to PARK funds with RBI and earn interest. The repo window is for banks that are SHORT of funds and need to borrow.

Value Addition:
• Memory anchor: Repo = banks need money → sell securities to RBI; Reverse Repo = banks have excess money → park it with RBI.
• The direction of securities flow: Repo: Bank → RBI (securities); RBI → Bank (cash). Reverse Repo: RBI → Bank (securities); Bank → RBI (cash).
• Post-SDF, banks parking surplus funds get no securities in return — the uncollateralised design of SDF.

solution.concept_anchor: 'Withdrawal of accommodation' ≠ rate hike — stance vs. rate are distinct signals

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: When the Monetary Policy Committee changes its stance to 'Withdrawal of Accommodation,' it signals that the next policy action will be a reduction in the policy repo rate to further support economic recovery.
statement_analysis.reason: Withdrawal of Accommodation signals the OPPOSITE — it indicates that the next action is unlikely to be a rate cut, and future moves will be tilted toward normalisation or tightening. It does NOT signal a rate reduction.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: A monetary policy stance of 'Accommodative' indicates that the MPC is biased toward rate cuts in future meetings, though it does not guarantee a rate reduction at every subsequent meeting.
statement_analysis.reason: Accommodative stance signals a cutting bias — the MPC is more likely to reduce rates than hold or hike in upcoming meetings. However, the stance is a directional signal, not a commitment to cut at every meeting.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Wait, correct option is (a): Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct = option (d). Let me recheck: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) S1 correct S2 incorrect, (d) S1 incorrect S2 correct. Statement 1 is incorrect; Statement 2 is correct. Correct option = (d). [Internal correction: correct_option must be d, not a. Updating.]
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: 'Withdrawal of Accommodation' signals a rate CUT — this is factually wrong. This stance signals that the MPC is moving away from easy policy; it implies next moves are not cuts. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: 'Accommodative' stance = cutting bias, not a guarantee of cuts at every meeting — this is precisely the correct interpretation of forward guidance. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — answer is option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the most common 'Withdrawal of Accommodation' misconception: students hear 'accommodation' and think removing the stance means doing the opposite (i.e., cutting rates to restore accommodation). In fact, the phrase means RBI is withdrawing ITS accommodative position — moving away from easy policy. The stance signals the MPC's bias for future actions, not a commitment to immediately reverse course. This is one of the most frequently tested monetary policy language traps in recent UPSC papers.
solution.final_explanation:
Monetary policy stance language is a separate testable dimension from rate decisions themselves.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: 'Withdrawal of Accommodation' does NOT signal a rate cut — it signals the opposite. The MPC is communicating that it intends to move away from its easy-money position. The next action under this stance is more likely to be a hold or hike than a cut. Students who read 'withdrawal = removing the tightening' make this error.
• Statement 2 — Correct: 'Accommodative' stance means the MPC has a bias toward rate cuts. However, forward guidance is a bias indicator — not a promise. The MPC may hold rates at an accommodative-stance meeting if incoming data warrants caution.

Value Addition:
• Stance spectrum (loosest to tightest): Accommodative → Neutral → Calibrated Tightening / Withdrawal of Accommodation.
• RBI adopted 'Withdrawal of Accommodation' in June 2022 and began rate hikes — but the stance itself preceded the first hike by a meeting.
• Forward guidance reduces market uncertainty — even without a rate change, a stance shift moves bond yields and exchange rates.

solution.concept_anchor: MSF allows borrowing against SLR securities — can dip into SLR holdings
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a ('MSF uses identical collateral to repo — G-Secs and T-Bills — but at a higher rate') is deceptive because G-Secs ARE eligible under MSF, but the distinguishing feature is that MSF also allows banks to DIP INTO their SLR holdings as collateral — something repo does not permit.
elimination_logic: Recall the key operational distinction of MSF: banks can borrow under MSF even by pledging securities from their SLR holdings — they can temporarily dip below the mandated SLR. Repo does not allow SLR securities to be used in this way.
Eliminate option a — while G-Secs are eligible under both, option a misses the SLR dipping feature that makes MSF uniquely flexible.
Eliminate option b — MSF provides liquidity TO banks (banks borrow from RBI), not the other way around. B reverses the direction.
Eliminate option d — MSF rate is NOT equal to the repo rate; it is Repo + 25 bps (higher than repo, forming the ceiling).

Option c correctly states the MSF's distinguishing feature: banks can borrow against their SLR-eligible securities, including by temporarily falling below their mandatory SLR, within prescribed limits.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option a is the entity-swap trap — it states G-Secs are the collateral (true, but incomplete) while omitting the SLR-dipping feature. Students who know 'both repo and MSF involve G-Secs' will select option a as 'close enough.' The precise distinction — that MSF allows banks to temporarily draw down their SLR portfolio as collateral in a way repo does not — is the targeted knowledge. This feature makes MSF a genuine emergency window; banks can access it even when their non-SLR security holdings are exhausted.
solution.final_explanation:
The Marginal Standing Facility is an emergency borrowing window designed for situations where banks face acute short-term liquidity stress beyond what normal LAF repo can address.

• Option (a): Incorrect — while G-Secs and T-Bills are eligible under MSF, this option omits MSF's defining feature: banks can borrow by dipping into their SLR portfolios (up to a specified limit), which repo does not allow.
• Option (b): Incorrect — MSF is a window through which banks BORROW from RBI, not the reverse. The direction of lending is Bank (borrower) ← RBI (lender).
• Option (c): Correct — MSF allows banks to borrow overnight at Repo + 25 bps and can use SLR-eligible securities as collateral, with the permitted facility of temporarily breaching SLR levels within defined limits.
• Option (d): Incorrect — MSF rate = Repo + 25 bps (the ceiling of the LAF corridor), not equal to the repo rate.

Value Addition:
• The limit up to which banks can dip into SLR securities under MSF has varied — RBI has increased/decreased this limit during liquidity stress events.
• MSF was raised temporarily during demonetisation (2016) and COVID (2020) to provide emergency liquidity headroom.
• Bank Rate = MSF Rate since 2012 — this is a frequently tested equivalence.

This is a plausible-fabrication trap — Malegam Committee sounds authoritative and 2014 is correct, but the attribution is wrong.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three) is the strongest distractor; statements 1 and 2 are correct and the false attribution in Statement 3 to 'Y.H. Malegam Committee' sounds plausible to students who cannot recall the exact committee name.
elimination_logic: Statement 3 attributes FIT and MPC recommendations to 'Y.H. Malegam Committee' — this is false. The Urjit Patel Committee (2014) made these recommendations. Y.H. Malegam is associated with microfinance sector reforms, not monetary policy. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Eliminate option (d) which includes Statement 3 as correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are both accurate — Urjit Patel Committee, single target, WACR as operational target.
Correct answer: 1 and 2 only = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Y.H. Malegam Committee is a real RBI committee (it reviewed microfinance regulations in 2011) — making it a plausible-fabrication distractor. Students who cannot recall 'Urjit Patel Committee' but know a Malegam Committee exists may accept the attribution as plausible. The fabrication combines a real committee name with a real year and real policy content, making it one of the harder entity-swap/plausible-fabrication combinations.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2014 Urjit Patel Committee was a landmark inflection point in India's monetary policy architecture.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Urjit Patel Committee recommended a single operating target framework centred on the repo rate, moving away from multiple rates and multiple indicators.
• Statement 2 — Correct: WACR (the call money overnight rate) became the operational target — RBI uses daily LAF operations to keep WACR anchored near the repo rate, making the overnight inter-bank market the 'transmission point.'
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The recommendation for FIT and the statutory MPC came from the Urjit Patel Committee (2014). The Y.H. Malegam Committee (2011) reviewed the microfinance sector following the Andhra Pradesh MFI crisis — it has no connection to FIT or MPC design.

Value Addition:
• Urjit Patel was RBI Deputy Governor (Monetary Policy) in 2014 and later became RBI Governor.
• FIT was formally legislated through RBI Act amendment in 2016 — two years after the committee's recommendation.
• WACR typically trades within 10–15 bps of the repo rate in normal liquidity conditions — evidence that the LAF corridor works.

solution.concept_anchor: Macroprudential tools vs. monetary policy — LTV, risk weights, sectoral caps
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (sectoral risk weight adjustments) sounds technical and niche; students may assume it belongs to monetary policy (since it is used to control credit) rather than recognising it as a macroprudential tool distinct from the repo rate.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: tools used to address asset price bubbles and financial system risks beyond CPI targeting — these are macroprudential tools used ALONGSIDE the repo rate, not via it.

Loan-to-Value ratio caps, Sectoral risk weight adjustments, and Counter-cyclical capital buffers are all macroprudential regulatory tools — they operate through banking regulation, not through the interest rate channel.
Open Market Operations is a monetary policy tool used for liquidity management (buying/selling G-Secs) — it does NOT address asset price bubbles through a regulatory/macroprudential channel.
OMO is the odd one out — it belongs to monetary policy/liquidity management, not macroprudential regulation designed for asset bubble control.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap works by listing three genuine macroprudential tools (LTV caps, risk weights, counter-cyclical buffers) with one monetary policy tool (OMO). Students who know 'repo rate is not used for asset price control' may be unsure about OMO's category — since OMO involves G-Secs and is conducted by RBI, it sounds like it could fit into the 'asset price management' set. The distinction: OMO manages liquidity (monetary policy); LTV/risk weights/buffers manage credit quality and systemic risk (macroprudential).
solution.final_explanation:
When RBI addresses asset price bubbles and financial stability risks beyond CPI targets, it uses macroprudential tools — a distinct toolkit from monetary policy rates.

• Option (a) — Loan-to-Value ratio caps: Macroprudential tool; limits how much banks can lend against collateral (e.g., housing). Belongs to this category.
• Option (b) — Open Market Operations: Monetary policy/liquidity management tool — RBI buys/sells G-Secs to inject or absorb liquidity. This does NOT target asset prices or financial stability risks through a regulatory channel. It is the ODD ONE OUT.
• Option (c) — Sectoral risk weight adjustments: Macroprudential tool; RBI increases the risk weight on, say, housing loans to make them costlier for banks to hold, cooling that sector. Belongs to this category.
• Option (d) — Counter-cyclical capital buffers: Macroprudential tool; banks build capital reserves during booms to absorb losses during busts. Belongs to this category.

Value Addition:
• LTV caps are set sector-by-sector (e.g., housing, gold loans) — RBI has periodically tightened and loosened them.
• Risk weight increases raise the capital requirement for specific loan categories without changing the overall repo rate.
• The Basel III framework introduced counter-cyclical capital buffers globally; India's implementation is coordinated by RBI.
